context.brief:
## Employee
- Name: SD (no id)
- Role: Process Engineer, Process
- Plant / unit: Bantu / Unit 100

## Equipment history in the knowledge graph
- none found for this profile; interview from the profile alone and ask them to name their key equipment

topics.title: Role and unwritten responsibilities of Process Engineer in Unit 100
topics.rationale: Understanding the full scope of SD's role beyond job description, including informal leadership and decision-making patterns.
seed_questions: What responsibilities have you taken on that aren’t in the official description?
How did you prioritize daily tasks when multiple issues arose simultaneously?
Who did you rely on most for cross-functional coordination, and why?

topics.title: Unit 100 process history and major modifications over the years
topics.rationale: Document significant process changes, bypasses, and de-bottlenecking projects that may not be fully documented.
seed_questions: What were the biggest process changes you oversaw?
Which modifications were temporary but never removed?
Why were some improvement projects started but not completed?

topics.title: Unwritten knowledge of Unit 100’s critical equipment
topics.rationale: No equipment records exist; SD must identify key assets and their failure patterns, workarounds, and maintenance quirks.
seed_questions: Which three pieces of equipment cause the most reliability headaches?
For each, what are the early warning signs of impending failure that you watch for?
Are there any non-standard repairs or temporary fixes that have become permanent?

topics.title: Undocumented operating envelopes and limit-breaking practices
topics.rationale: Process engineers often know safe limits beyond design and how to push them. Capture those boundaries.
seed_questions: When the unit runs at 110% capacity, what do you monitor most closely?
Are there any instrumentation readings you distrust and compensate for mentally?
What conditions have led to near-miss events that aren’t in the incident system?

topics.title: Tribal knowledge about process upsets and recovery
topics.rationale: SD likely carries informal playbooks for upset conditions that aren’t in formal trouble-shooting guides.
seed_questions: Describe a serious upset that isn’t well documented – what happened and how did you recover?
What manual interventions does the board operator perform that are not in the procedures?
Who are the go-to people (internal or external) when things go wrong, and why?

topics.title: SOP gaps and procedural workarounds in Unit 100
topics.rationale: Some standard procedures may be outdated or missing steps known only to experienced staff.
seed_questions: Which start-up or shutdown steps are routinely done differently from the written SOP?
Have you ever bypassed a safety interlock? Under what circumstances?
Are there batch or recipe adjustments that operators make based on your verbal instructions?

topics.title: Vendor, contractor, and lab relationship quirks
topics.rationale: Personal relationships and unwritten knowledge about external parties can affect unit performance.
seed_questions: Which equipment vendor’s field service engineer do you trust most, and why?
Are there analytical results you always double-check because the lab’s method is unreliable?
Which contractors understand the unit’s idiosyncrasies, and who should never be hired again?

topics.title: Half-finished projects and open modifications in Unit 100
topics.rationale: Capture the status of incomplete work that could create risk or wasted effort if not understood.
seed_questions: What improvement projects are in limbo right now?
Why were they paused or not completed?
What’s the minimal effort to get them to a safe, operable state?

topics.title: Control system tuning and alarm management secrets
topics.rationale: PID tuning values, alarm setpoints, and suppression strategies are often only in the engineer’s head or personal notes.
seed_questions: Which control loops have you retuned, and what are the final parameters?
Are there alarms that are routinely suppressed or ignored, and why?
Have you developed any custom trends or calculation blocks that aren’t documented?

topics.title: Handover: Top risks and advice for the successor
topics.rationale: Succession planning requires identifying immediate risks and unwritten knowledge needed to run the unit safely.
seed_questions: What keeps you awake at night about Unit 100 after you leave?
If you could give your successor only three pieces of advice, what would they be?
Are there any deteriorations or near-miss patterns that will likely escalate in the next six months?

topics.title: Informal coordination with Operations and Maintenance
topics.rationale: The engineer’s effectiveness often depends on relationships and informal communication channels.
seed_questions: How did you typically negotiate priorities with the shift supervisor?
What maintenance requests did you fast-track by talking to the planner directly, and why?
Are there operators whose instinct you trust more than instrument data?

topics.title: Essential reference documents and personal files
topics.rationale: SD may have personal spreadsheets, marked-up P&IDs, or notes that contain critical data not in the official repository.
seed_questions: What files or notebooks do you have that your successor absolutely needs?
Are there any P&IDs you annotated with corrections that were never updated?
Which engineering calculations or spreadsheets do you rely on most?

transcript.text: SD, thank you so much for making time to sit down with me today. I know you're heading into retirement soon, and honestly, there's a lot of knowledge in your head about Unit 100 that probably isn't written down anywhere. That's exactly what I want to capture before you go. So let me start with a broad question: if you could sit your replacement down and tell them just one thing — what would you say is the most important thing to know about running Unit 100?
